messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Visual test system
parts:
Hi all -

I've been working on a visual testing system for ggplot2. The basic idea is that you run the visual tests and store the resulting images in the git repo; then at any later time you can re-run the tests and it will (A) tell you if anything changed, and (B) visually display the changes. I started writing it up here:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Visual-test-system

Hopefully it'll reduce the number of bugs that enter the ggplot2 codebase, by helping us catch them right away.


Here are some web pages that are automatically generated by the system. These are probably more exciting to look at than the wiki page above.
This one shows the results from a test run:
http://stdout.org/~winston/visual_test/html/aspect-ratio/

This one compares the current test results to those from a previous commit in the repo:
http://stdout.org/~winston/visual_test/diff/diff/visual_test/aspect-ratio/



Feedback is welcome!
-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Visual test system
parts:
I hadn't heard of it before. I looked into how tools::compactPDF actually works, and it appears to use qpdf, which is a command-line utility included with R (at least it is on the Mac distribution of R).

I did some experimentation with qpdf, turning off compression because the output files should be text rather than compressed binary files. The compression results in savings for each file, but I think I ran this on PDF files generated by ggsave:
  qpdf --stream-data=uncompress in.pdf out.pdf
It appears to take off 6KB of the file size for small files and large ones. The small files were scatterplots of mtcars data (15094 --> 8815 bytes), and the large ones were scatterplots of diamonds data (4084909 --> 4078631)


Next I compared the git storage efficiency of raw PDFs vs. those processed with qpdf without compression, vs. those processed through qpdf with compression. I added 67 PDFs from visual tests to new git repositories. I made three new git repositories with the PDFs processed in different ways:
1. raw
2. qpdf --stream-data=uncompress
3. qpdf --stream-data=compress

Then I ran 'git gc --aggressive' to clean up the repo. The final sizes of the .git/ directories were almost the same:
1. raw: 155,861 bytes
2. qpdf, uncompress: 155,642 bytes
3. qpdf, compress: 207,322 bytes

So using qpdf with compression results in a larger repo size. Using qpdf without compression results in a barely smaller repo, and it saves 6KB per file in the working tree. I'm thinking that the modest savings are probably not worth the extra complexity...

-Winston

A few comments:
- "Each description must be unique, otherwise the filenames will be the same, and some of test image files will be overwritten." : there should be a check and a warning on that because I suspect this will happen (coming up with good names is difficult).
Good idea.
- adding a "watch" system (such as auto_test() in testthat) would be a welcome future development

That would be cool. I haven't used auto_test before, so I'm not sure exactly how it works. For these tests, it would have to be intelligent and not run all the tests all each time. This might be hard because ggplot2 is sufficiently complicated that it's hard to tell what is code affects what tests.
Also, I habitually press ctrl-S a lot, so it would have to be smart enough to cancel running tests and start over when a file is updated.
- how does that integrate into R's package testing architecture? If if doesn't, it would be great to think of ways to make it work.

It doesn't at the moment...
I know there's a package called graphicsQC by Paul Murrell which might be used for that stuff, but it seemed kind of a heavy-weight solution, and didn't integrate with git as far as I could tell.


I had a thought about how to store the test images. It is of course possible to store them in the master branch. The drawback is that it's impossible to ever remove the test images from the repository. Also, this doesn't record information about the last time someone ran the tests -- if the test images come out unchanged, then there's nothing to commit, and no record of it in the repository.

One alternative is to store the test images in side branches. For example, make a branch off 0.9.0 called 0.9.0-vtest, run the tests, and commit them to that branch. These side branches could be made off any commit, and they would inherently record information about which commit was tested. They could also be deleted from the repository, freeing up space if that ever becomes an issue. The one drawback I can think of is that it could clutter up the branch namespace. It's kind of unorthodox, but it's worth considering.


-Winston

You mean that currently they are stored in the ggplot repo itself? I thought there were in their own repo. I would, personally at least, prefer this option because adding image will quickly bloat the ggplot repo and clutter its history.

If you want to have a centralized place for testing, so that several people can contribute tests and corresponding images, then this repo can be made public and shared. Overall, a possible setup could be:
- one repo/package for ggplot
- one repo/package for the visual test code
- one repo for the vtest results on each graphics package (starting with ggplot)

Keeping track of the version (of ggplot2 or or other graphic packages) that is tested could be done by:
- adding a text file with the hash of the head of ggplot, or (better) a unified way to get a version number from R (that would be incremental also for devel versions, maybe something date-based). Every time a test is run, even if there is no visual change, the version number is incremented. The file could even store a text representation of the test with an OK or failed/modified status to highlight the failures.
- tagging each commit in the images repo with the hash/version number of the head of ggplot. In that case, the version number of the package tested is only recorded when there is a difference.
In both cases, maybe a post-commit hook could be set on the master branch in the ggplot repo (by Hadley) to run all visual tests after each commit; or maybe a post-push hook to allow to work incrementally on a feature without having to switch to a branch.

Anyhow, congratulations again, this looks very polished of a first stab at it.

Yes, it could actually be separated from ggplot2. It initially was meant to be just another feature of ggplot2, but it's gotten to the point where it might make sense to put it in another package.

I want to make sure I have the fundamental stuff straightened out before actually using it for anything real. This includes, for example, the layout of the directories, the naming of files, the required structure of the test scripts, and the vtest() function, since these parts determine how people set up their test systems, and will affect their repositories. Other things like the vdiff functions are not so fundamental, since they don't affect anything permanent -- they just provide a way of viewing the information.

> One alternative is to store the test images in side branches. For example, make a branch off 0.9.0 called 0.9.0-vtest, run the tests, and commit them to that branch. These side branches could be made off any commit, and they would inherently record information about which commit was tested. It's kind of unorthodox, but it's worth considering.

You mean that currently they are stored in the ggplot repo itself? I thought there were in their own repo. I would, personally at least, prefer this option because adding image will quickly bloat the ggplot repo and clutter its history.

That's correct, they're stored in the repo. I think the problem of repo bloat isn't as bad as it might seem at first. I found that storing uncompressed PDFs results in the git repo has surprisingly good efficiency, as I described in an earlier message.

That said, it's not a requirement for the test images to be part of the ggplot2 repo. You could keep all the tests in a completely separate repository.

If you want to have a centralized place for testing, so that several people can contribute tests and corresponding images, then this repo can be made public and shared. Overall, a possible setup could be:
- one repo/package for ggplot
- one repo/package for the visual test code
- one repo for the vtest results on each graphics package (starting with ggplot)

Something could work. The idea of letting people push to a vtest repo is interesting, but I think then, instead of having each commit in the vtest repo be a test set, you'd want to have a separate directory storing tests for each commit (and perhaps R version and OS platform). It would be kind of cool if you could add to the vtest repo by doing something like this:
$ cd vtest
$ git pull
$ R
> vtest()
> quit()
$ git add 0a09ac88/2.14.2/mac/  # This is where the new tests were saved
$ git commit
$ git push

The idea is that it would create a directory like 0a09ac88/2.14.2/mac/ (or something more sophisticated like you described) and put all the visual test results in there. Then you could push to the repo and submit a pull request if someone else maintains the "central" vtest repo. The size of the git repo itself would be small since there's a lot of copies of the same data (ideally the images don't change), but the on-disk size of the working tree would grow relatively quickly.

So that's one way to have a distributed testing platform backed by git. It wouldn't require a customized central server; any public git repo will do.

But all this is probably more than ggplot2 needs at this point...

Keeping track of the version (of ggplot2 or or other graphic packages) that is tested could be done by:
- adding a text file with the hash of the head of ggplot, or (better) a unified way to get a version number from R (that would be incremental also for devel versions, maybe something date-based). Every time a test is run, even if there is no visual change, the version number is incremented. The file could even store a text representation of the test with an OK or failed/modified status to highlight the failures.
- tagging each commit in the images repo with the hash/version number of the head of ggplot. In that case, the version number of the package tested is only recorded when there is a difference.
In both cases, maybe a post-commit hook could be set on the master branch in the ggplot repo (by Hadley) to run all visual tests after each commit; or maybe a post-push hook to allow to work incrementally on a feature without having to switch to a branch.

Anyhow, congratulations again, this looks very polished of a first stab at it.

Pretty webpages can give that impression. ;)  I borrowed the look from Hadley's staticdocs.

-Winston

This sequence of commands makes me think that it would be very nice if you could encapsulate the git commands into R functions (which could do something clever to ensure the commits are valid etc.).

> The idea is that it would create a directory like 0a09ac88/2.14.2/mac/ (or something more sophisticated like you described) and put all the visual test results in there. How would you diff if you have a separate directory per ggplot commit?

Do you expect a lot of differences between versions of R and OSes? It seems it would complicate quite much an initially lean design. I'd say that if, at some point, there are consistent differences between OSes you would want to separate them in a branch, but ultimately, the goal should be to have identical output everywhere (and merge or drop the branches). Versions of R would probably be less of a problem because ggplot used to require the latest version of R and since updates are easy and free, you can expect users to upgrade.

In any case, if you want to keep subdivisions (by OS, version etc.) branches are probably the way to go: they are stored efficiently and don't take additional space in the working copy too. And you also probably want an easy way to diff between two arbitrary versions (whether they are in separate directories or branches)
> So that's one way to have a distributed testing platform backed by git. It wouldn't require a customized central server; any public git repo will do.
Having this (i.e., "a distributed testing platform backed by git") as a goal, in a general context (not just for ggplot) strikes me as a very good objective.

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Visual test system
parts:
> $ cd vtest
> $ git pull
> $ R
> > vtest()
> > quit()
> $ git add 0a09ac88/2.14.2/mac/  # This is where the new tests were saved
> $ git commit
> $ git push

This sequence of commands makes me think that it would be very nice if you could encapsulate the git commands into R functions (which could do something clever to ensure the commits are valid etc.).

That would be convenient, but I'm kind of wary of doing stuff that modifies the git repository from within R. There are a lot of things that can happen even with a git pull (e.g., you have a dirty working tree, or local and origin have diverged, or you're on some other branch) and it's hard to prepare for all those contingencies.

> The idea is that it would create a directory like 0a09ac88/2.14.2/mac/ (or something more sophisticated like you described) and put all the visual test results in there. Then you could push to the repo and submit a pull request if someone else maintains the "central" vtest repo. The size of the git repo itself would be small since there's a lot of copies of the same data (ideally the images don't change), but the on-disk size of the working tree would grow relatively quickly.

How would you diff if you have a separate directory per ggplot commit?
This would have to be handled differently from how it's done right now. Right now it uses git because it's easy, but it would be possible to check for changes without using git.

Do you expect a lot of differences between versions of R and OSes? It seems it would complicate quite much an initially lean design. I'd say that if, at some point, there are consistent differences between OSes you would want to separate them in a branch, but ultimately, the goal should be to have identical output everywhere (and merge or drop the branches).

I don't expect to see differences across platforms, since I think R's PDF code is the same on all platforms (I could be wrong, though).

I agree that it would complicate things a lot... The nice thing about the way it works now is that the history of the tests is linear, and tracks the history of the code base. Once you add in different platforms, it becomes more complicated to manage. It's probably not worthwhile for ggplot2 at this point.
And you also probably want an easy way to diff between two arbitrary versions (whether they are in separate directories or branches)

It actually supports this now for test results committed to the git repo. you just give vdiff_webpage() any two git commit refs. For example, you could do something like:
  vdiff_webpage("ggplot2-0.8.9", "HEAD")
You could also use branch names or SHA1 hashes referencing a specific commit.



Returning to the issue of storing test results, I still like the idea of 
creating a side branch, or side branches. This allows for "time traveling", the ability to retroactively store test results from old code. It also allows you to delete old test results from the repo, something that's impossible if the test results are stored in the main line.

Right now I could, for example, check out 0.8.9, run visual tests, and commit the results to a vtest-0.8.9 branch. Then I could check out 0.9.0, run the same tests, and commit them to a vtest-0.9.0 branch. I could compare these results against each other, or I could use either as a reference that I test against when doing development. If I later realize I want to add more tests to 0.8.9 to use as reference images, I could checkout vtest-0.8.9, add the new tests, run them, and commit. But this may be more complexity than it's worth.

The nice thing with the visual test code is that it can work with any storage model, as long as it's backed by git. And if it's useful, non-git-backed storage models could be added.

-Winston
